820.title: Digging in the desert
820.hook: a caravan out of water; a boy hammers through the rock and finds it (Jataka 2)
820.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell this tale to encourage effort, viriya, one of the perfections, especially to people who have grown discouraged in their practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two caravans, one pouring out its water on a stranger's word, one checking the sky. Your line: keep the water. Today, a caravan that has already run dry.

The sand is too hot to cross by day, so the caravan travels at night, steered by a guide who reads the stars. Late in the journey, the guide falls asleep. The oxen wander, turn, and walk all night in a circle. At dawn the merchants see their own campsite from yesterday. Their water and firewood are gone. That's where the second tale of the Jataka begins: lost, dry, and back at the start.
screen: `TRAVELING BY THE STARS.` → `THE GUIDE FALLS ASLEEP.` → `BACK AT THE START.`

segments.voice: First, the despair. The caravan people lie down under their carts and give up. The leader, the bodhisatta, thinks: if I give up too, everyone dies. So while it's still cool, he walks the camp, looking. Second, the grass. He finds a clump of kusa grass growing in the sand. Grass means water somewhere below, he reasons. He has the men dig, deep into the ground, until the spades hit rock. Nothing. The men drop their tools. Third, the listening. The bodhisatta climbs down into the pit and lays his ear against the stone. Underneath, faintly, he hears water running. He turns to a serving boy. If you give up, he tells him, we're all lost. Go down with the hammer, and strike the rock. Fourth, the boy. The boy goes down when the grown men have quit. He swings the hammer, again and again, and the rock splits. Water rises up the shaft, the tale says, as tall as a palm tree. Everyone drinks, cooks, rests, and travels on. The frame story is about a monk who'd given up on his practice, and the Buddha tells him this tale to remind him that in a past life he was the boy with the hammer. Look at who saves the caravan. Not the leader, not the men with the spades. A serving boy, doing one more swing.
screen: `THEY LIE DOWN AND GIVE UP.` · `GRASS, A PIT, THEN ROCK.` · `AN EAR AGAINST THE STONE.` · `THE BOY SWINGS ONCE MORE.` · then, large: `DIG ONCE MORE.`

segments.voice: Picture one thing you stopped working on because it hit rock: a project, a conversation, a habit. Don't promise to finish it; just listen, the way the bodhisatta listened through the stone, for anything running underneath. If something is there, name one small swing you could take; if not, that's information too, so rest.
Viriya. Effort, energy: what a boy showed, swinging a hammer until the water came, after a lost caravan's pit hit rock. Today's word.
Your line: dig once more. Sometimes the water is just one more swing away. Rest well.

821.title: A dead mouse
821.hook: a young man turns a dead mouse into a fortune by steady small trades (Jataka 4)
821.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the tale of the little treasurer as an encouragement to begin practice with whatever is at hand and keep at it steadily.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a boy's viriya, one more swing, and the water came. Your line: dig once more. Today, a fortune that starts with something nobody wants.

A dead mouse is lying in the street. A wealthy treasurer, on his way to the king, glances down and says out loud: a sharp young man could pick that up and start a business. A passerby might laugh. One young man, poor and standing close enough to hear, doesn't laugh. He picks the mouse up. That's the fourth tale of the Jataka, and the treasurer is the bodhisatta.
screen: `A MOUSE IN THE STREET.` → `A REMARK IN PASSING.` → `ONE MAN PICKS IT UP.`

segments.voice: First, the mouse. The young man sells it at a tavern, as food for the cat, for one tiny copper coin. That's the whole starting capital. Second, the trades. With the coin he buys a bit of molasses and a jar of water. He waits for the flower gatherers coming home hot and tired, gives them a drink and a taste of sweetness, and they give him flowers. He sells the flowers, and does it again. After a storm, he gathers fallen branches from the king's garden and sells the wood to a potter. He gives water to the grass cutters, and later, when horse dealers come to town, the grass cutters sell him their grass. Each step is tiny; none is clever on its own. Third, the patience. Bit by bit, watching what people need and waiting for the moment, the young man becomes rich. Not by luck: by a long line of small, honest trades, each paying for the next. Fourth, the return. He goes back to the treasurer whose remark started it all, brings him a gift and tells him the story. The treasurer, delighted, gives him his daughter in marriage, and in time the young man takes his place as treasurer. The Jataka tells it for a monk who'd been slow and discouraged at the start, and its point is spiritual as much as financial: steady small effort, started with whatever is lying in front of you, adds up.

segments.voice: Pick something you've wanted to begin and haven't, because you don't have enough yet: time, money, skill. Look for the dead mouse, the smallest plain piece already in front of you, like five minutes or one page. Name that one piece, let it be enough for today, and rest with the breath.
Starting capital. The dead mouse a poor young man sold for one coin, the whole starting capital that steady small trades turned into a whole new life. Today's word.
Your line: from a dead mouse. Small honest steps, each paying for the next. Until tomorrow.

822.title: The dancing peacock
822.hook: a peacock dances without modesty and loses his bride (Jataka 32)
822.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the Nacca Jataka as a lesson in restraint and a sense of shame, hiri and ottappa in Pali.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a dead mouse, sold for one coin, the starting capital of a whole new life. Your line: from a dead mouse. Today, someone who already has everything, and throws it away in a minute.

Every bird in the mountains has gathered in one place. The king of the birds, a golden goose, has promised his daughter she may choose her own husband, and she walks along the rows of feathered hopefuls. She stops in front of the peacock, with his jewel-colored neck and patterned tail, and says: that one. In the Nacca Jataka, that should be the end. It's the beginning of his mistake.
screen: `ALL THE BIRDS GATHER.` → `SHE CHOOSES HER OWN.` → `SHE CHOOSES THE PEACOCK.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. Long ago, the tale says, the four-footed animals made the lion their king, the fish chose a great fish, and the birds chose the golden goose. His daughter asks one wish: to pick her husband herself. He agrees, and calls the assembly. Second, the choice. She picks the peacock. The other birds bring him the news, and he's so thrilled, so eager to show what he's got, that he says: she hasn't even seen my dancing yet. Third, the dance. Right there, in front of the king, the bride, and every bird in the mountains, the peacock spreads his feathers wide and dances. He's so busy showing off that he forgets himself and loses every bit of modesty, in the middle of the crowd. Fourth, the cost. The golden goose is embarrassed for everyone. He speaks a verse: your voice is pleasant, your back is lovely, your neck has the color of a jewel, but for that dance I won't give you my daughter. He has no shame inside and no restraint outside, the king says, and gives his daughter to a young goose, his own nephew. The peacock flies off, ashamed. The tale never says he was ugly, or unworthy, or unloved. He'd already been chosen. The win was finished, and the urge to prove it is what undid it. The Jataka tells it for a monk who forgot restraint in front of everyone.
screen: `A LION, A FISH, A GOLDEN GOOSE.` · `SHE PICKS THE PEACOCK.` · `HE DANCES IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.` · `GIVEN TO THE YOUNG GOOSE INSTEAD.` · then, large: `THE DANCE COST HIM.`

segments.voice: Recall a place where you're tempted to show off: a meeting, a dinner table, a post you're about to share. Notice the little lift in the chest, the urge to make sure everyone sees, and without scolding it, feel it rise and pass the way a breath does. Whatever is already settled can stay settled.
Modesty. What the peacock lost, dancing to show off after he was already chosen, and so lost the bride he'd already won. Today's word.
Your line: the dance cost him. What's already won doesn't need a dance. Day eight hundred twenty-two, done.

823.title: Who is eldest
823.hook: a partridge, a monkey and an elephant decide by the banyan tree who should be honored (Jataka 37)
823.howItsDone: In Buddhist monastic communities, monks and nuns are seated and greeted in order of seniority since ordination, and lay Buddhists may greet elders with a bow.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the peacock danced away his modesty, and the bride he'd already won. Your line: the dance cost him. Today, three friends who need to sort out who goes first.

A partridge, a monkey and an elephant share a home under a great banyan tree. They're friends, more or less, but they keep stepping on each other: nobody listens, nobody defers, nobody knows whose word should count. So they agree on a fix. Whoever is oldest gets the honor, and the others will listen to him. Except none of them knows who that is. The Tittira Jataka is how they find out.
screen: `THREE FRIENDS, ONE TREE.` → `NOBODY DEFERS.` → `BUT WHO IS OLDEST?`

segments.voice: First, the elephant. When I was young, he says, this banyan was a little bush. I walked right over it, and its top branches brushed my belly. Second, the monkey. When I was young, I'd sit on the ground and nibble this banyan's topmost shoots without even stretching my neck. Third, the partridge. There used to be another great banyan, over in another place. I ate one of its fruits, and dropped the seed right here. This tree grew from that. So I knew this tree before it was a tree at all. The other two agree at once: the partridge is the eldest. From then on they honor him and listen to his advice, and the tale says they lived well together. Each claim is a memory, and the oldest memory wins. Fourth, the frame. In the present-day story, the Buddha hears that his senior disciple Sariputta spent a night outside, because younger monks had taken every place to sleep. He tells this tale, and teaches that in the community, places and respect go by seniority in the order, not by birth or status. Honor here isn't flattery. It's a way of making room, so a crowded home under one tree can get along.
screen: `THE ELEPHANT: A BUSH I WALKED OVER.` · `THE MONKEY: I ATE ITS TOP SHOOTS.` · `THE PARTRIDGE: I DROPPED THE SEED.` · `SARIPUTTA SLEPT OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `HONOR THE ELDEST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who was there before you, a grandparent, a teacher, a neighbor, a longtime colleague, someone who remembers the tree as a seed. Hold their face for a few breaths. Then picture one small way to give them a place, like asking their advice or letting them speak first.
Seniority. What a partridge, a monkey and an elephant settle by the oldest memory of their tree, and the partridge wins. Today's word.
Your line: honor the eldest. The oldest memory belonged to the smallest bird. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 823 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CRANE AND THE CRAB.`

824.title: The crane and the crab
824.hook: a crane promises fish a better lake and eats them, until the crab (Jataka 38)
824.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the tale of the crane and the crab as a warning that deceit can turn back on the deceiver.

segments.voice: Yesterday: three animals settled seniority by memory, and the partridge won. Your line: honor the eldest. Today, a promise that sounds wonderful.

It's the hot season, and the pond is shrinking. The fish can feel the walls of mud closing in. On the bank, a crane stands very still, looking sad on their behalf. He's been worrying about them, he says. He knows a big lake not far off, deep, cool, full of lotuses, and he'd be glad to carry them there, one at a time. Free of charge. In the Baka Jataka, the fish have an answer ready.
screen: `A POND DRYING UP.` → `A SAD-LOOKING CRANE.` → `A BETTER LAKE, FREE.`

segments.voice: First, the doubt. The fish tell the crane plainly: we've never heard of a crane who cared about fish. You want to eat us. So the crane offers proof: send one of you to see the lake. They pick a big fish, blind in one eye, and the crane really does carry him there, lets him swim, and brings him back. It's real, the fish tells everyone. Second, the trap. Now the fish line up, and one at a time the crane carries each off, but not to the lake. He flies to a tree beside it, pins the fish in a fork of the branches, and eats it. The pile of bones under the tree grows. Third, the crab. At last only a crab is left. The crane offers him the same trip. Yes, says the crab, but I'd better hold your neck with my claws so I don't fall. On the way, the crab sees the tree and the bones, and the crane says it out loud: I'm going to eat you too. Fourth, the grip. The crab squeezes. Take me to the water, he says, or I'll take your head. The choking crane sets him down at the lake's edge, and the crab snips through his neck anyway. A tree spirit who watched it all, the bodhisatta in this tale, speaks a verse: guile doesn't profit the guileful; look what the crane got from the crab. The crab never trusted the offer. He held on.
screen: `ONE FISH SENT TO CHECK.` · `A TREE, A PILE OF BONES.` · `THE CRAB HOLDS THE NECK.` · `THE TRICKSTER MEETS THE CRAB.` · then, large: `THE CRAB REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Pick one offer in your life that sounds wonderful: a deal, a message, a person saying they'll take care of everything. Ask the fishes' question, does this kind of helper usually care about me, and then the crab's, where's my grip if it turns out wrong? No need to decide anything; just hold both questions gently and breathe.
Baka. Crane or heron: the bird whose sweet offer ate every fish, until a crab kept hold of its neck. Today's word.
Your line: the crab remembers. A sweet offer can still have bones under its tree. Day eight hundred twenty-four.

825.title: The monkey gardeners
825.hook: monkeys water the saplings by pulling each one up to check its roots (Jataka 46)
825.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the Aramadusaka Jataka as a lesson that good intentions need wisdom too, and that checking too soon can do harm.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the baka, the crane, and a crab who held on. Your line: the crab remembers. Today, helpers who mean well, and ruin everything.

There's a festival in the city of Benares, crowds in every street, and the king's gardener badly wants to go. But the young trees in the royal park need water while he's away. A troop of monkeys lives in the park; they eat the fruit and enjoy the shade, so surely they owe him a favor. He goes to their king and asks. The monkey king says: of course. Leave it to us.
screen: `A FESTIVAL IN THE CITY.` → `THE SAPLINGS NEED WATER.` → `LEAVE IT TO US.`

segments.voice: First, the job. The gardener hands over the water skins and wooden pots and goes off to the festival. The monkey king tells his troop to water the young trees. Second, the plan. But water is precious, the monkey king says. We mustn't waste it. So before you water a tree, pull it up and look at its roots. Long roots get a lot; short roots get a little. It's careful, thrifty, and sounds like good management. Third, the result. The monkeys go through the park, pulling each sapling out of the ground, inspecting the roots, and watering accordingly. Every young tree they check, they kill. Fourth, the witness. A wise man walking through the park, the bodhisatta in this tale, asks what they're doing. Their king's orders, they explain. And he says, in a verse, that the ignorant, trying to do good, do harm instead, like the monkeys in the king's garden. What makes the tale sharp is that nobody is wicked. The monkeys aren't lazy or greedy. They're conscientious. They wanted to be sure, and being sure meant digging up the very thing that needed to stay in the dark to grow. A root does its work out of sight.
screen: `THE GARDENER GOES TO THE FESTIVAL.` · `CHECK THE ROOTS, SAVE THE WATER.` · `EVERY TREE THEY CHECK DIES.` · `HARM FROM TRYING TO HELP.` · then, large: `DON'T PULL UP THE ROOTS.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind something young in your life: a plan, a friendship, a skill, someone you're helping along. If you've been pulling it up to check its roots, measuring it, asking if it's working yet, picture setting it back in the ground and patting the soil down. Water it, leave it alone, and breathe.
Conscientious. What the monkey gardeners were, careful helpers who pulled up every sapling to measure its roots, and killed what they meant to save. Today's word.
Your line: don't pull up the roots. Good intentions need wisdom too. Until next time.

826.title: The virtuous elephant
826.hook: an elephant rescues a lost man, who comes back to saw off his tusks (Jataka 72)
826.tomorrow: The fish who prayed for rain
826.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the Silavanaga Jataka as a picture of generosity and patience that don't depend on gratitude, and as a warning about where ingratitude leads.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the monkey gardeners, so conscientious they pulled up every sapling. Your line: don't pull up the roots. Today, kindness that keeps going after it's been betrayed.

A man from Benares has gone into the forest for work and lost his way. He wanders, crying out in fear. Then a huge white elephant steps out of the trees. The man runs. The elephant stops. The man stops. The elephant steps forward; the man runs again. At last the man understands: this animal means no harm. He's the bodhisatta, the tale says, and he's come to help.
screen: `A MAN LOST IN THE FOREST.` → `A WHITE ELEPHANT APPEARS.` → `HE COMES TO HELP.`

segments.voice: First, the rescue. The elephant takes the man home, feeds him on fruit, and carries him on his back out of the forest to the road. But as they go, the man quietly notes every tree and hill along the way. Second, the bargain. Back in Benares, he walks down the street of the ivory carvers and asks what they'd pay for the tusks of a living elephant. A lot, they say. So he takes a saw and goes back. Third, the gift. He tells the elephant he's poor, with nothing to live on. Would he give him his tusks? The elephant kneels and lets him saw. He gives them freely, saying it isn't that he doesn't value them: the wisdom he is seeking is dearer to him. The man sells them, then comes back for the stumps. The elephant gives those too. Then he comes a third time and digs out the roots of the tusks. Each time, the elephant lets him. Fourth, the end. As the man walks away, the tale says, the earth splits open and swallows him. A tree spirit speaks a verse: give an ungrateful man the whole world, and it still won't satisfy him. The tale never calls the elephant foolish. He gives three times, each gift costing more, and the tale saves its judgment for the taker. The man's ingratitude doesn't get to decide who the elephant is. The tale's last line names the man as Devadatta, whose ingratitude toward the Buddha is the story's frame.
screen: `CARRIED OUT OF THE FOREST.` · `THE STREET OF THE IVORY CARVERS.` · `TUSKS, THEN STUMPS, THEN ROOTS.` · `THE EARTH OPENS.` · then, large: `GOOD TO THE UNGRATEFUL.`

segments.voice: Remember a time someone took your help and gave nothing back; not the deepest wound you carry, a small one. Forgiving isn't approving, so just see if you can set the weight of it down for a moment, the way the elephant knelt. Breathe out, and let your kindness belong to you, not to them.
Sila. Virtue, good conduct: what the virtuous elephant showed, rescuing a lost man, then giving him tusks, stumps and roots, and staying good to the end. Today's word.

Your line: good to the ungrateful. The week in lines: dig once more, from a dead mouse, the dance cost him, honor the eldest, the crab remembers, don't pull up the roots. Day eight hundred twenty-six, done.
